comments.author: Chazut
comments.body_html:
No, ORBIT doesn’t change how bots spawn or get grouped, that’s still up to SPT and your spawn mod (ABPS). Solo spawns stay solo, duos stay duos.

What ORBIT does is take whatever groups the spawn system gave you and:

  • Assign each one a small list of goals at spawn (loot zone, PvP hotspot, EFT quest)
  • Coordinate the members internally (leader takes the anchor, others spread to nearby loot/cover, the bot who got the kill is the one sent to loot the body)
  • Manage their looting, doors, and extracts

So you won’t suddenly see “squads everywhere”, just more deliberate behaviour from the groups already spawning.

Thanks, glad it runs clean.

Both are multipliers, not meters. Every map has its own tuned convergence radius baked in and the slider just scales it: 1.0 = the map default, 2.0 = double the reach. The actual meters vary per map (big open maps reach way further than tight ones), that’s why it’s a scale and not a fixed distance.

I was reading through today’s comments—I follow this mod, so I get notified whenever someone replies—and I saw the author being criticized for using AI, or more specifically, for allegedly not being transparent enough about it.

Honestly, I don’t really understand the argument. The source code is publicly available. Anyone is free to inspect it, audit it, or even fork the project and build their own version. Regardless of how much AI was involved in writing the code, as long as the author has personally reviewed every part of it, stands behind what was shipped, and confirms there is nothing malicious or deceptive in it, I don’t see that as a problem.

AI is just another tool. We shouldn’t diminish an author’s creativity simply because better tools have become available. Modding itself is built on expanding and reimagining someone else’s work, and many successful modders are self-taught rather than formally trained software engineers. Years ago, people learned from forum posts, tutorials, and each other. Today, AI has simply become another assistant in that learning and development process. What really matters is the ability to turn an idea into something people can actually enjoy.

As long as AI isn’t replacing the author’s creative direction or decision-making, I don’t think the exact percentage of AI-generated code is particularly meaningful. In a non-commercial modding community, debating whether AI wrote 30%, 60%, or 90% of the code feels like missing the point. If anything, AI lowers the barrier to entry and allows more creative people to bring their ideas to life, which ultimately benefits the community as a whole.

And honestly, that’s a future I’d rather embrace than resist.
